summary: A humorous parody of the Christmas carol The Twelve Days of Christmas, listing the endless gripes of computer support work, such as broken databases and failing hardware. It is an informational memo, with no technical content.

plainLanguage.summary: A funny holiday song where, every day, the gifts are more computer problems.

subtitle: A Christmas carol about network and database disasters

tldr.problem: Every day brings a new crisis in tech support: broken databases, network failures, difficult users, licensing nightmares, and hardware drama.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC is a parody of The Twelve Days of Christmas, with each verse adding a new tech disaster to an ever-growing list, starting with a broken b-tree and escalating through transceivers, SCSI drives, modems, and licensing collapse.
tldr.outcome: A humorous vent that, despite being written as a joke, captures real pain points in 1990s technology operations.

today: RFC 1882 is Informational and has never been updated. It stands as a historical and humorous snapshot of 1990s technology operations.

sections.title: A Humorous Memo
sections.content: RFC 1882 is not a technical standard; it is humor published in an informational memo. The author parodies The Twelve Days of Christmas to catalog the chaos of network operations in the mid-1990s. Each day introduces a new category of disaster, from the first day's database corruption to the twelfth day's crisis symphony: modem security violations, license violations, user confusion, hardware failures, support-line despair, and infrastructure breakdowns all happening together.
sections.plainLanguage: A tech support worker wrote a funny song about everything that breaks at once during a bad week.

sections.title: The Disasters
sections.content:
The RFC catalogs 12 categories of disaster, each repeating and growing: a database with a broken b-tree, transceiver failures causing packet storms, difficult users, support calls held in eternal queue, SCSI disk problems, software licensing expiration, games consuming bandwidth, modem security breaches, executive demanding fixes, SNMP alerts, fried circuit boards, and misconfigured virtual pipes. Each refrain includes asides capturing the frustration: "Rebuild WHAT? It's a 10GB database!" and "CTL-ALT-DEL is not the proper way to end a program."

The final verse combines all twelve disasters at once, suggesting that December is when everything fails simultaneously.
sections.plainLanguage: The song lists twelve different kinds of computer problems, each one getting more and more annoying, and by the end all twelve are happening at the same time.

sections.title: Still True Today
sections.content: Though written in 1995, the RFC captures timeless tech operations challenges: cascading failures, support fatigue, licensing confusion, security gaps, and the human friction between technical staff and end users. Many of these problems—broken databases, network diagnostics, licensing audits, security incidents, and overbooked infrastructure—remain familiar to network operations teams decades later.
sections.plainLanguage: Even though this was written in 1995, the problems it jokes about still happen to computer networks today.
